To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pigeons' choice accuracy in delayed matching is a joint function of the sample duration and the predictability of the duration.

(1) sample duration has no effect on delayed matching performance unless it is correlated with the sample appearing and/or with the reinforced choice alternative, and (2) when sample duration is correlated with the reinforced alternative, the effect of sample duration is determined by its ability to provide information about the relative reduction in delay to reinforcement.
pigeons' delayed-matching performance is affected by sample duration, and that the effect is mediated by the extent to which sample duration is correlated with reinforcement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of conditioned reinforcement in the development of stimulus control in delayed matching.
the question of whether or not a sample stimulus, in the context of a delayed matching task, can be a conditioned reinforcer.
the question of whether or not pigeons can use the temporal duration of a visual sample as a basis for choice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sample duration effects are not simply the result of the sample duration itself, but rather the result of the relative reduction in delay that is signaled by the sample.
pigeons' matching performance is a function of the relative reinforcing properties of the samples, which are themselves a function of their relative duration.

sample-duration effects in the pigeon are not simply due to the passage of time per se but are a function of the predictability of the sample duration and its correlation with the relative delay to reward.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

pigeons are sensitive to the overall delay reduction provided by sample stimuli, and that this sensitivity can be expressed in terms of conditional reinforcement, as well as in terms of the effects of sample duration on the discriminability of comparison alternatives.

the effects of sample duration are not a simple function of sample duration, per se, but are also a function of the degree to which the duration itself is a signal that the delay to reinforcement will be reduced.
the effects of sample duration on matching are determined by the extent to which it is correlated with the delay to reinforcement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sample duration itself is not a cue for choice in delayed matching, and that its effects depend on its association with reinforcement.
the sample duration effect is not a function of the absolute duration of the sample, per se, but rather of the relative reduction in delay to reinforcement that it signals.
the effects of sample duration on delayed matching are not solely a function of the sample's ability to cue the correct comparison choice.
